# Mockingbird

**Realistic mocks of the APIs your code calls, generated by an LLM from their contracts, consistent for the whole session, and reached without changing a line of your app.**

[![CI](https://github.com/RJ-s-Org/Mockingbird/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/RJ-s-Org/Mockingbird/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/RJ-s-Org/Mockingbird?include_prereleases&sort=semver)](https://github.com/RJ-s-Org/Mockingbird/releases)
[![License: MIT OR Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%20OR%20Apache--2.0-blue)](#license)
[![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-mdBook-informational)](docs/README.md)

![A terminal session: a bookshop mock mapped to api.bookshop.example, and an unchanged Node app run with `mockingbird run` that lists real-looking books with EUR prices, creates an order, reads it back from session state and gets the 404 the contract declares](docs/assets/demo.gif)

Give Mockingbird an OpenAPI, GraphQL, protobuf, WSDL or AsyncAPI contract and it serves a mock whose answers read like production data: names, prices, timestamps and ids that fit together, in your contract's exact shape. Create an order and the next `GET` returns that order. Ask for a 404, a slow response or a flaky upstream and you get it in the API's own error format. Run your app under `mockingbird run` and its calls to `api.stripe.com` or `api.github.com` land on the mocks, with no base URL to change.

## Why it is different

- **Realistic, and always valid.** An LLM writes each answer from the operation, the request, the session's state and your persona; Mockingbird validates it against the schema, patches small errors locally and falls back to a schema-valid faker when the model misbehaves. Every response says where it came from (`X-Mockingbird-Source: state | cache | llm | repaired | fallback`). `--offline` needs no key at all.
- **Stateful without scripting.** Writes change the session's state; reads of what you created are answered from it, lists seed later reads by id, and repeated reads are cached. Sessions are isolated by a header, and can be exported, seeded and reset as fixtures.
- **Zero-edit proxy.** Give a mock the real host names it stands in for (`hosts: [api.stripe.com]`), and the built-in HTTPS proxy, with its own local CA, routes the app's traffic to it. `mockingbird run -- npm start` sets it all up for one command.
- **Every protocol from one binary.** REST, GraphQL (with subscriptions), gRPC (all four call kinds, with reflection), SOAP 1.1/1.2, server-sent events, WebSocket, and AsyncAPI channels on Kafka, AMQP and MQTT. No contract? [Smart import](docs/import.md) drafts one from documentation, a HAR file or a Postman collection.
- **Agent-native.** `mockingbird mcp` is an MCP server whose tools cover the whole product, with skills and plugins for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Kiro, VS Code, Windsurf and ChatGPT. Ask your agent to "mock the Stripe API for this app" and it can.
- **Ready for a team.** Scenarios, chaos, signed webhooks, a console with OIDC and RBAC, an audit log, Postgres or Redis state, and a Helm chart with an HA split between control and data planes.

## Sixty-second quickstart

Install (macOS and Linux; Windows: `irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rj-s-org/mockingbird/main/install.ps1 | iex`):

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rj-s-org/mockingbird/main/install.sh | sh
```

Run your app against mocks of the APIs it calls. Map each mock to the host it replaces in `mockingbird.yaml`:

```yaml
mocks:
  stripe:
    contract: ./stripe-openapi.json   # github.com/stripe/openapi, spec3.json
    hosts: [api.stripe.com]
    persona: A small online bookshop in Berlin; prices in EUR.
```

```sh
mockingbird run -- npm start            # an LLM writes the answers (set a key: `mockingbird init` lists providers)
mockingbird run --offline -- npm test   # no key, no network: the built-in faker answers
```

Or serve a contract and call it yourself:

```sh
mockingbird serve --offline fixtures/openapi/orders-3.0.yaml

curl -s -XPOST localhost:8080/orders -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"customerId":"c1","total":10}'
curl -s localhost:8080/orders/<id>                              # the order you just created
curl -s localhost:8080/orders/<id> -H 'X-Mockingbird-Status: 404'   # the contract's own 404
```

The [Quickstart](docs/quickstart.md) covers LLM providers, the background server, config files and ports; [Concepts](docs/concepts.md) explains sessions, sources and scenarios.

## How it compares

Each of these tools is good at what it was built for. This table describes their open-source editions from their own documentation as of October 2026; [open an issue](https://github.com/RJ-s-Org/Mockingbird/issues) if something is out of date.

| | Mockingbird | [WireMock](https://wiremock.org) | [Prism](https://stoplight.io/open-source/prism) | [Mockoon](https://mockoon.com) | [Microcks](https://microcks.io) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where answers come from | An LLM, from the contract and session, validated against the schema; faker fallback | Stubs you write (with Handlebars templating), or recordings | Examples in the OpenAPI document, or schema-based random data | Routes you define, with templating and faker | Examples in the contracts or Postman collections; dispatch scripts |
| Protocols | REST, GraphQL, gRPC, SOAP, SSE, WebSocket, Kafka, AMQP, MQTT | HTTP (REST, SOAP); gRPC and GraphQL through extensions | HTTP from OpenAPI 2/3 | HTTP, WebSocket | REST, GraphQL, gRPC, SOAP, AsyncAPI (Kafka, MQTT, AMQP, WebSocket, NATS and more) |
| State across calls | Automatic per session: creates, updates and deletes are remembered | Scenario state machines you define | None | Data buckets and CRUD routes | Scripted, with a key-value store |
| Without a contract | Drafts one from docs, HAR or Postman, for review | Record and playback | Needs OpenAPI | Build routes by hand, or import OpenAPI | Needs contracts or collections |
| Reaching the mock | Base URL, or a forward proxy that intercepts HTTPS for mapped hosts | Base URL, or browser proxying with HTTPS interception | Base URL; a validation proxy in front of a real API | Base URL; forwards unmatched routes to a real API | Base URL |
| Runs as | One Rust binary, Docker, Helm | Java, Docker | Node CLI, Docker | Desktop app, CLI, Docker | Server with UI, Docker, Kubernetes operator |
| License | MIT or Apache-2.0 | Apache-2.0 | Apache-2.0 | MIT | Apache-2.0 |

Choose WireMock or Mockoon when you want exact, hand-authored responses; Prism when your OpenAPI examples are the source of truth and you want request validation; Microcks for contract testing across many teams' APIs. Choose Mockingbird when you want realistic, consistent data from a contract without writing stubs, across protocols, and an app that runs against it unchanged.

## Integrations

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **CI** | [GitHub Action](integrations/github-action), GitLab CI, snapshot replay without an LLM key: [CI guide](docs/ci.md) |
| **Infrastructure as code** | Terraform / OpenTofu provider and Pulumi: [IaC guide](docs/iac.md) |
| **Kubernetes** | [Helm chart](deploy/helm/mockingbird) (`oci://ghcr.io/rj-s-org/charts/mockingbird`), Argo CD and Flux: [Kubernetes](docs/deploy/kubernetes.md), [GitOps](docs/deploy/gitops.md) |
| **Tests** | Testcontainers: [module](integrations/testcontainers), [throwaway mocks for a test run](docs/deploy/gitops.md#4-throwaway-mocks-for-a-test-run); fixtures with `export-fixtures` / `seed-fixtures`: [CLI](docs/cli.md) |
| **Coding agents** | `/plugin marketplace add rj-s-org/mockingbird` in Claude Code, or `mockingbird agent install <codex\|cursor\|gemini\|kiro\|vscode\|windsurf\|claude-desktop>`: [Coding agents](docs/agents.md) |
| **Containers** | `ghcr.io/rj-s-org/mockingbird` (full and `-slim`, signed with cosign): [Docker](docs/deploy/docker.md) |

## Examples

The [examples catalog](docs/examples.md) mocks about twenty well-known APIs, each ready to serve with one command. The [example gallery](examples/gallery/README.md) has one small configuration per protocol family and one for chaos.
